problem: Prior LLM-based Minecraft agents (Voyager, STEVE) are single-agent or naively parallelised free agents, with inefficient inter-agent communication, task distribution and global perception; they cannot handle image, audio and object goals in one system.
motivation: Open-ended Minecraft navigation needs multi-agent coordination and multi-modal goal understanding. Simply adding more free agents gives limited gains, so the authors argue for a hierarchical, human-like organizational structure with a shared global view.
key_idea: A manager MLM plans centrally with a dynamic global map and auto-organizes conductor/action-agent groups that execute in a decentralized way, backed by multi-modal retrieval memory.
insight: The ablations show that both the dynamic map and the auto-organizing mechanism matter. Removing auto-organizing (w/o AO) hurts multi-agent block search (106 blocks vs 367) and map area (706 vs 1368). Removing the dynamic map (w/o DM) hurts goal search (success 0.64 vs 0.93 multi-agent) and block search. HAS with a single agent already beats single-agent baselines, which the authors attribute to layered task decomposition.
method: Hierarchical CPDE: a manager MLM does centralized planning, and conductors deploy action agents for decentralized execution (inspired by CTDE in MARL).
Manager modules: Planner, Describer, Critic and Deployer; the Describer converts images and audio to text.
Conductor modules: Actor, Curriculum, Critic and Skill; conductors create and adjust action-agent groups per subtask.

Auto-organizing and intra-communication: the manager spawns conductors dynamically (AutoAgents-like, SOG-inspired); action agents talk only to their conductor, which summarizes and redistributes messages.
Multi-modal memory: key-value memory of successful plans, with retrieval-augmented planning and top-k retrieval through Describer text descriptions.
Dynamic map: a global image map that is the union of all agents' explored areas, updated in real time and used by the manager for planning.
Adaptive planning: multi-modal observations are converted to text (STEVE-21K keywords plus GPT-4 sentences); plans are corrected via closed-loop feedback and simulated step by step.

setting.training_data: none (training-free); STEVE-21K keywords and environment seeds used for description and evaluation
setting.observation: Minecraft first-person vision plus audio (given as text intensity/range) and other properties (biome, inventory), and a shared dynamic map
setting.privileged: Audio goals are simulated as text of perceptible range and feedback intensity around the target; baselines rely on backend text information

numbers.eval_set_note: at least 30 tests per task, over 15 seeds of 6 terrains
numbers.evidence: Table 1: HAS (Ours) 8/7/3 agents, Image Goal 6 iters, 0.84

numbers.extra: peak 3 agents; audio simulated as text

numbers_note: Custom Minecraft tasks, not standard navigation benchmarks; no standard-benchmark numbers. Table 1 single-agent and multi-agent rows differ, and the agent counts listed are per goal.
results: HAS beats Voyager and STEVE on every task, including with a single agent. With multiple agents: image-goal SR 0.84 vs 0.52 (STEVE); object-goal SR 0.95 vs 0.59 (Voyager); block search 367 blocks vs 211 (STEVE); map exploration area 1368 vs 755 (Voyager, 5 agents).
limitations: Evaluated only in custom Minecraft tasks against two adapted baselines, with no standard navigation benchmarks; audio is simulated as text
Depends on GPT-4V, with no reported cost or latency analysis, and the number of agents is capped at 8
Sparse method and implementation details, and thin ablations with no statistical variance reported
